question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
title: Single Responsibility Principle Explained
direct_answer: SRP states that a class should have only one reason to change — meaning it should encapsulate exactly one responsibility. If a class handles user logic, email sending, AND database persistence, any of those three concerns can force a change, making the class fragile and hard to maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why separation of concerns matters at the class level and can articulate the 'one reason to change' concept.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defining SRP vaguely as 'do one thing' without explaining what 'one reason to change' means in concrete terms.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete before/after example showing how splitting a class reduces coupling and makes the codebase easier to maintain.

sections.title: Understanding Single Responsibility Principle
sections.content:
The **Single Responsibility Principle** is the first principle of SOLID, stating that a class should have **only one reason to change**. This doesn't mean a class can only do one thing — it means all the things it does should relate to a single, well-defined responsibility.

Think of it like a restaurant: a waiter takes orders, a chef cooks, a cashier handles payment. If the waiter also cooked and managed finances, any change to menu preparation, payment processing, or service style would force changes to the waiter's duties — making the role fragile. In code, when a **UserController** handles HTTP requests, validates input, sends emails, AND writes to the database, changes to email templates, validation rules, database schema, or REST endpoints all require modifying the same class. This creates a maintenance nightmare. SRP says: split those concerns so each class has **one axis of change**. The principle protects you from **shotgun surgery** (one feature change requires touching many unrelated classes) and makes each class easier to understand, test, and modify independently.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|One Reason to Change|~SRP core rule|class owns a single concern|change in one concern → one class edited|the 'S' in SOLID
blue|Violation Smell|~god class|HTTP + DB + email in one class|name has 'And' or 'Manager'|unrelated imports mixed
emerald|The Fix|~split by concern|Controller / Service / Repository|each class one axis of change
violet|Payoff|~maintainability|smaller blast radius|easier to test and read

sections.title: SRP Violation vs Compliant Design
When to Apply SRP
sections.content:
Apply SRP when designing any new class — ask yourself: **what is this class's single job?** Use it when you catch yourself writing a class that needs imports from multiple unrelated packages like javax.mail, java.sql, and org.springframework.web in the same file.

Apply SRP during code reviews when you see method names that hint at multiple concerns: saveAndEmail(), validateAndStore(), or parseAndNotify(). It's especially critical in **service layers** where it's tempting to mix business logic, persistence calls, external API calls, and notification logic. In Spring Boot apps, SRP naturally emerges when you use **@Service** for orchestration, **@Repository** for data access, and separate utility classes for formatting or validation. If a class is hard to name without using 'And' or 'Manager', it likely violates SRP and needs splitting.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing SRP with 'one method per class'**: Freshers often think SRP means tiny classes with single methods, leading to absurd over-granularity. A UserRepository with save, findById, delete is perfectly SRP-compliant because all methods serve one responsibility: User data access.
- **Naming classes with vague suffixes**: Using names like UserManager, DataHandler, or ServiceHelper hides the real responsibility. These become dumping grounds for unrelated methods.
- **Mixing layers in one class**: Putting @RestController, business logic, and @Repository annotations on the same class violates SRP by mixing presentation, domain, and persistence concerns. Each layer is a separate reason to change.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **One reason to change**: A class should change only when its single responsibility needs modification, not when unrelated concerns change
**Cohesion over method count**: Ten methods serving one responsibility is better than three methods serving three responsibilities
**Package imports as a smell**: If your class imports javax.mail, java.sql, and javax.xml together, it's likely violating SRP
**Testability improvement**: SRP classes have fewer dependencies to mock and narrower test surfaces, making unit tests simpler
**Layer separation**: In Spring Boot, @Controller, @Service, and @Repository naturally enforce SRP at the architectural level
**Refactoring trigger**: When you struggle to name a class without 'And' or 'Manager', consider splitting it by responsibility
**Prevents shotgun surgery**: Changes to one concern don't ripple through classes handling unrelated concerns

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have only one reason to change. That means all the code in that class should relate to a single, cohesive responsibility. It's not about limiting methods — a UserRepository can have save, find, update, and delete methods because they all serve one responsibility, which is managing User data access. The key idea is about change. If you have a class that handles HTTP requests, validates input, sends emails, and writes to the database, then changes to REST endpoints, validation rules, email templates, or database schema all force you to modify that same class. That's fragile. You want each class to change for only one reason. In a Spring Boot app, you'd apply SRP by separating concerns into layers. Your controller handles HTTP, your service handles business logic, your repository handles data access, and maybe you've got a separate email service for notifications. That way when the database schema changes, you only touch the repository. When business rules change, you only touch the service. One pitfall freshers fall into is thinking SRP means one method per class, which would make your codebase unmanageably granular. Focus on one responsibility, not one method. If all the methods in a class serve the same concern, you're good.

question: How do you identify an SRP violation in existing code?
title: Identifying SRP Violations in Java Code
direct_answer: SRP violations are visible when a class has multiple unrelated reasons to change — large file size, names containing 'And', or imports from unrelated packages like javax.mail AND java.sql. The real test: ask 'why would this class change?' — more than one independent answer means SRP violation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to spot design smells in real codebases beyond just theoretical knowledge.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only giving theoretical signs without practical detection strategies like counting imports or analyzing method signatures.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention class size, number of imports, instance variables, or the 'why would this change' test as concrete signals.

sections.title: Detecting SRP Violations in Real Code
sections.content:
Identifying **SRP violations** requires looking beyond surface-level code to understand what forces changes to a class.

The core technique is asking: **'Why would this class need to change?'** — if you get multiple independent answers ("when email templates change", "when database schema changes", "when business rules change"), you've found a violation. Concrete signals include **class file length** (>300 lines is suspicious), **import diversity** (mixing java.sql, javax.mail, org.json in one class), **method signature variety** (some methods return domain objects, others return void for side effects), and **instance variable count** (>7 fields often means multiple concerns). Look for method names with **'And'** like saveAndEmail() or validateAndNotify() — these scream multiple responsibilities.

In Spring Boot apps, check if a single class has multiple stereotypes implied by its behavior: does it handle HTTP, execute business logic, AND query the database? Another smell is **frequent modification** — if every feature request touches the same class, it's likely a God Object violating SRP. The 'change test' is the most reliable: imagine common changes (UI redesign, database migration, external API integration) and see how many classes each affects.

sections.title: Identifying SRP Violations Through Code Smells
When to Apply Detection Techniques
sections.content:
Use detection techniques during **code reviews** before merging pull requests — SRP violations compound quickly if not caught early.

Apply the 'why would this change' test when **onboarding to a legacy codebase** to identify refactoring targets. Run static analysis during **technical debt sprints** to find large classes (>300 lines), high cyclomatic complexity (>10), or classes with many dependencies. In Spring Boot projects, check for classes mixing **@RestController with @Repository** logic or services with embedded SQL queries. When debugging **flaky tests**, SRP violations often surface as tests that break for unrelated reasons because the class under test has too many dependencies.

Use import analysis when a class imports from more than **three distinct top-level packages** — that's a red flag for mixed concerns. During **refactoring sessions**, prioritize classes that appear in multiple unrelated bug reports or feature stories — they're likely violating SRP and need splitting.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only checking line count**: Freshers often think any large class violates SRP, but a 400-line UserRepository with 30 cohesive data-access methods is fine, while a 150-line class mixing HTTP, business logic, and email is a violation. Size is a smell, not proof.
- **Ignoring import diversity**: Not noticing when a class imports from javax.mail, java.sql, and org.springframework.web — that combination is a clear signal of mixed concerns.
- **Accepting vague class names**: Letting classes named ServiceHelper, DataManager, or OrderHandler pass review without questioning what responsibility those names actually describe. These become dumping grounds for unrelated code.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **The change test**: Ask 'why would this class change?' — multiple independent answers indicate SRP violation
**Import diversity smell**: Classes importing from unrelated packages like javax.mail, java.sql, org.json likely mix concerns
**Method name patterns**: Names containing 'And' like saveAndEmail or validateAndNotify are red flags for multiple responsibilities
**Instance variable count**: More than 7 fields often indicates a class managing multiple unrelated concerns
**Class length threshold**: Files over 300 lines warrant investigation, though line count alone doesn't prove violation
**Frequent modification pattern**: Classes appearing in many unrelated feature stories or bug fixes likely violate SRP
**Stereotype mixing**: Classes with behavior suggesting multiple Spring stereotypes (controller + repository logic) violate SRP

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The best way to identify an SRP violation is to ask why would this class change. If you get multiple independent answers, that's your signal. For example, if a class would change when the database schema changes, when email templates change, and when REST API contracts change, it's clearly doing too much. Beyond that test, there are concrete code smells to look for. Check the imports at the top of the file. If you see javax.mail, java.sql, and org.springframework.web all imported in the same class, that's mixing presentation, data access, and notification concerns. Look at method names — anything with And in it like saveAndEmail or validateAndNotify is usually handling multiple responsibilities. Check the instance variable count. If a class has more than seven or eight fields, especially of very different types like DataSource, MailSender, and ObjectMapper, it's probably managing multiple concerns. File size is another smell. A 400-line class isn't automatically bad if all the code is cohesive, but anything over 300 lines deserves a closer look. One pitfall is confusing large with wrong. A repository with thirty data-access methods might be large but perfectly compliant with SRP because all those methods serve one responsibility. Focus on diversity of concerns, not just size.

question: How does SRP improve testability of Java classes?
title: SRP and Unit Testability in Java
direct_answer: SRP improves testability because a class with one responsibility has fewer dependencies to mock and a narrower test surface. When a class does three things, a unit test must set up mocks for all three concerns even when testing only one — SRP eliminates that overhead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Connection between design principles and practical testing outcomes — whether you see design as enabling testing, not just code organization.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying SRP is only about code organization without linking it to concrete testing benefits like reduced mock setup.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete example comparing setup for a 3-dependency class vs three 1-dependency classes, highlighting mock count difference.

sections.title: How SRP Enables Easier Testing
sections.content:
The **Single Responsibility Principle** dramatically improves testability by reducing the **dependency surface** of each class. When a class has one responsibility, it needs fewer collaborators, which means fewer **mocks** or **stubs** to set up in unit tests.

Consider a UserService that validates input, saves to a database, and sends emails — testing just the validation logic still requires mocking the database and email dependencies because they're coupled into the same class. That's **test setup overhead** with no benefit. With SRP, you'd split this into ValidationService, UserRepository, and EmailService. Now testing validation requires **zero mocks** — it's a pure function. Testing the orchestration layer (the service that calls all three) requires mocks, but each individual concern is independently testable. SRP also creates a **smaller blast radius** for test failures: when a test breaks, you immediately know which responsibility is broken. In multi-responsibility classes, a test failure could be due to any of the intertwined concerns, requiring detective work to isolate the cause. Testability isn't just convenience — it's a forcing function for good design. If a class is hard to test, it's usually doing too much.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Fewer Dependencies|~SRP effect|one concern → few collaborators|fewer mocks to set up
blue|Pure Logic|~zero mocks|validator = input/output asserts|no DB or email stubbing
emerald|Isolated Failures|~clear signal|broken test → known responsibility
violet|Smell|~test pain|setup longer than the test → split it

sections.title: Testing SRP-Compliant vs Violating Classes
When Testability Drives SRP Application
sections.content:
Apply SRP for testability when you find yourself writing test setup that's **longer than the test itself** — that's a signal the class has too many dependencies.

Use it when tests become **brittle**, failing for reasons unrelated to the logic being tested because of tangled concerns. In Spring Boot projects, apply SRP when you need to use **@SpringBootTest** for logic that should be unit-testable — integration tests are slow and indicate design problems. When practicing **TDD** (Test-Driven Development), SRP violations surface immediately: if you can't write a simple test without complex mocking, the design needs adjustment before writing implementation.

Apply SRP in **service layers** where orchestration logic shouldn't be tangled with validation, transformation, or persistence details. If you're using Mockito and find yourself calling when().thenReturn() more than three times in one test, that's a smell indicating the class under test has too many responsibilities and needs splitting for better testability.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking SRP is only about code organization**: Freshers often see SRP as purely aesthetic, missing the concrete testing benefit — fewer mocks, faster tests, clearer failure messages. SRP is a practical enabler, not just theory.
- **Over-mocking in tests instead of fixing design**: When tests require many mocks, freshers often accept the pain and write complex test setup instead of recognizing it as a signal to split the class. The test pain is feedback about design.
- **Mixing integration and unit test concerns**: Testing a class that mixes business logic with database access using @SpringBootTest instead of recognizing the class violates SRP and should be split so logic is unit-testable with plain JUnit.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Reduced mock count**: SRP classes have fewer dependencies, meaning unit tests require fewer mocks or stubs to set up
**Isolated test failures**: When a test breaks in an SRP-compliant class, you immediately know which single responsibility failed
**Pure logic testability**: Classes with pure business logic and no dependencies require zero mocks, just input-output assertions
**Test setup as a smell**: If test setup is longer than the test itself, the class likely violates SRP and has too many dependencies
**Integration test avoidance**: SRP lets you unit-test logic without needing @SpringBootTest, making tests faster and more focused
**TDD compatibility**: Test-Driven Development naturally enforces SRP because multi-responsibility classes are painful to test-first
**Mockito threshold**: Needing more than three when-thenReturn calls in one test often indicates the class does too much

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: SRP improves testability because classes with one responsibility have fewer dependencies to mock. When you're writing a unit test, every dependency the class has is something you need to mock or stub. If your class does three things — say it validates input, saves to a database, and sends an email — you have to mock the database and email service even when you're only testing validation logic. That's wasted setup. With SRP, you'd split those into separate classes. Now your validation class has zero dependencies, so you can test it with plain assertions and no mocks at all. That's way simpler and faster. Beyond reducing mock count, SRP makes test failures clearer. When a test breaks in a multi-responsibility class, you have to figure out which of the tangled concerns caused it. In an SRP-compliant class, the failure immediately points to the single responsibility that broke. In Spring Boot projects, SRP lets you write fast unit tests instead of slow integration tests. If you need @SpringBootTest to test business logic, that's usually a sign the class is mixing concerns and violates SRP. One pitfall is accepting complex test setup as normal. If your test has ten lines of mock configuration before one line of actual assertion, that's feedback that your class needs splitting. The test pain is telling you something about the design.

question: What is the difference between SRP and separation of concerns?
title: SRP vs Separation of Concerns in Java
direct_answer: Separation of Concerns is the broad architectural principle that different concerns should be handled by different parts of the system — it applies at every level. SRP is SoC applied specifically at the class level, stating each class should encapsulate exactly one concern. SRP is a concrete application of SoC.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding — can you distinguish related principles and explain how they relate hierarchically?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating SRP and SoC as identical or using them interchangeably without recognizing the scope difference.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give examples at different levels: layered architecture or package structure for SoC, class design for SRP, showing the hierarchy.

sections.title: Distinguishing SRP from Separation of Concerns
sections.content:
**Separation of Concerns (SoC)** is a broad architectural principle stating that different concerns — like business logic, data access, presentation, security — should be handled by distinct parts of the system. It applies at **every level**: microservices vs monoliths, layered architecture, package structure, and class design. **Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)** is SoC applied specifically at the **class level**, stating each class should have exactly one reason to change.

Think of SoC as the overarching philosophy and SRP as one concrete implementation of that philosophy in object-oriented design. In a Spring Boot application, SoC manifests as the three-tier architecture: controllers handle HTTP concerns, services handle business logic, repositories handle data access. Within that architecture, SRP ensures each **individual class** serves one concern. A UserController shouldn't contain SQL queries (violates SRP), and the entire service layer shouldn't be in one package with repositories (violates SoC at package level). SoC is about **structural organization** across the system; SRP is about **responsibility assignment** within individual classes. Both aim to reduce coupling and increase cohesion, but at different granularities.

blue|Single Responsibility|~class-level|one reason to change|SoC applied to one class
emerald|Granularity|~different scope|SoC: packages and layers|SRP: classes and methods
violet|Together|~complementary|SoC builds the structure|SRP fills it with focused classes

One class handling HTTP and SQL

sections.title: When to Apply Each Principle
sections.content:
Use **Separation of Concerns** when making architectural decisions: should we split into microservices? How do we organize packages? Should frontend and backend be separate repos? Apply SoC when defining **module boundaries**, deciding what goes in the service layer vs the controller layer, or structuring packages like com.app.domain, com.app.infrastructure, com.app.api.

Use **SRP** when writing or reviewing individual classes: does this UserService class belong in the business layer or is it mixing data access? Should validation logic live in the controller or a separate validator class? Apply SRP during **refactoring** when you find classes that are hard to name or test. In Spring Boot projects, SoC guides your use of annotations like @RestController, @Service, @Repository to enforce layer separation. SRP guides what methods go in each of those annotated classes. Both principles work together: SoC creates the container structure, SRP fills it with well-designed classes.

Use SoC for the 30,000-foot view, SRP for the 10-foot view.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating SRP and SoC as synonyms**: Freshers often use the terms interchangeably, missing that SoC is the broad architectural principle and SRP is one specific application at the class level. This leads to confusion when discussing design at different scales.
- **Applying SRP without SoC**: Writing classes that each have one responsibility but organizing them poorly — like putting all service classes and repository classes in one giant package with no layer separation, which violates SoC.
- **Over-focusing on SRP and ignoring SoC**: Obsessing over individual class design while ignoring system-level organization, resulting in a codebase of perfectly designed classes in a chaotic structure with no clear architectural layers or package boundaries.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Scope hierarchy**: SoC is system-wide, SRP is class-level — SRP is one way to implement SoC in object-oriented design
**Different granularities**: SoC addresses modules, layers, and services; SRP addresses individual classes and their methods
**Complementary, not redundant**: SoC creates the architectural structure; SRP ensures quality within that structure
**SoC in Spring Boot**: Manifests as @RestController for web, @Service for business, @Repository for data layers
**SRP in Spring Boot**: Ensures each annotated class has one cohesive responsibility within its layer
**Violation at different levels**: Mixing web and data layers violates SoC; one class doing HTTP and SQL violates SRP
**Design decisions**: SoC guides package and module structure; SRP guides class and method design

sections.title: Code Example
How to Answer
sections.content: Separation of Concerns is the big-picture architectural principle that different concerns in your system should be handled by different parts. It applies at every level — whether you're splitting into microservices, organizing packages, or designing layers. SRP is that same idea applied specifically at the class level. It says each class should have one reason to change, meaning one well-defined responsibility. Think of SoC as the container and SRP as what goes inside. In a Spring Boot app, SoC is why you have separate controller, service, and repository layers. Each layer handles a different concern — HTTP in controllers, business logic in services, data access in repositories. That's architectural separation. SRP then says within each layer, every individual class should be focused on one responsibility. Your UserRepository should only do data access for User entities, not also send emails or validate input. Both principles aim to reduce coupling, but at different scales. SoC is about organizing modules and layers. SRP is about organizing classes and methods. You need both. One mistake freshers make is treating them as the same thing and using the terms interchangeably. Another is focusing only on class design with SRP while ignoring system-level organization with SoC, which gives you well-designed classes in a chaotic structure. Use SoC for architecture, SRP for implementation.

question: Can a class have multiple methods and still follow SRP?
title: Multiple Methods and SRP Compliance in Java
direct_answer: Yes — a class can have many methods and still follow SRP as long as all those methods serve the same single responsibility. A UserRepository with save, findById, delete, and update has four methods but one responsibility: data access for User. Method count is irrelevant; concern count is what matters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you truly understand SRP vs naive 'one method per class' misinterpretation that would make code impractical.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking SRP means a class should have only one method, which would lead to absurdly granular classes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish clearly between method count and responsibility count, giving examples of cohesive multi-method classes.

sections.title: SRP and Method Count Are Independent
sections.content:
The **Single Responsibility Principle** is about **concern count, not method count**. A class can have ten, twenty, or fifty methods and still perfectly comply with SRP — as long as all those methods relate to the same single responsibility.

Consider a **CustomerRepository** with methods like save, findById, findByEmail, findByLastName, update, delete, existsById, and count. That's eight methods, but they all serve one cohesive responsibility: **data access for Customer entities**. The class has one reason to change: when the way we store or retrieve Customer data changes. Contrast this with a three-method class that validates input, sends an email, and logs to a database — despite having only three methods, it violates SRP because those three concerns are unrelated and would change for independent reasons. The word 'single' in Single Responsibility refers to having **one axis of change**, not a limit on functionality. Think of **cohesion**: all methods in an SRP-compliant class collaborate toward the same goal. A naive interpretation that restricts classes to one method would force you to create hundreds of tiny classes with names like UserSaver, UserFinder, UserDeleter — making navigation and understanding the codebase nightmarish. SRP is about **semantic unity**, not artificial size constraints.

sections.title: Multi-Method Classes Following SRP
When Multi-Method Classes Are Appropriate
sections.content:
Multi-method classes are appropriate when all methods serve a **cohesive responsibility** — repositories, validators, formatters, calculators, and adapters naturally have many methods.

Use them in **repository patterns** where CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) plus query variations all relate to data access for one entity.

Apply in **service orchestration** where multiple public methods represent different workflows but all coordinate the same domain concern. In **utility classes**, many static helper methods for one data type (StringUtils with trim, capitalize, truncate, format) are fine. Multi-method classes shine in **Spring Data JPA** repositories where you define findByX, findByY, existsByZ — all querying the same entity type. The key test: **if you removed half the methods, would the class name still make sense?** If your UserValidator lost validateEmail but kept validatePassword and validateAge, it's still a validator. That's cohesion.

Avoid multi-method classes when methods operate on **different data types** (one method takes Orders, another Customers) or have **unrelated side effects** (some methods query databases, others send HTTP requests, others write files).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing method count with responsibility count**: Freshers often think SRP means one method per class, leading to absurd over-granularity like UserSaver, UserFinder, UserDeleter classes instead of one cohesive UserRepository with all related methods.
- **Accepting utility dump classes**: Allowing classes like Utils, Helper, or Manager to grow to hundreds of methods serving unrelated purposes just because 'SRP allows multiple methods.' Those violate SRP because the methods don't share a single responsibility.
- **Forcing artificial splits**: Breaking a cohesive 15-method repository into five separate classes just to reduce method count, which increases complexity without any design benefit and makes the codebase harder to navigate.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Cohesion over count**: Ten methods serving one responsibility is better than three methods serving three unrelated concerns
**Responsibility definition**: SRP's 'single' refers to one reason to change, not a limit on functionality or method count
**Repository example**: A repository with save, findById, update, delete, exists, count is perfectly SRP-compliant
**Semantic unity test**: All methods should collaborate toward the same cohesive goal, like data access or validation
**Naming test**: If you removed half the methods, would the class name still describe what remains? If yes, it's cohesive
**Anti-pattern**: Creating UserSaver, UserFinder, UserDeleter instead of one UserRepository violates pragmatism
**Utility classes**: Classes like StringFormatter with many static methods are SRP-compliant if all format strings

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Yes, absolutely. A class can have many methods and still follow SRP. The principle is about having one responsibility, not one method. Method count is irrelevant. What matters is whether all those methods serve the same cohesive concern. A good example is a repository. A UserRepository might have save, findById, findByEmail, update, delete, exists, and count. That's seven methods, but they all do the same thing: manage data access for User entities. The class has one reason to change — if the database schema changes or we switch databases, all those methods might need updating, but they change together because they're part of the same responsibility. Contrast that with a class that has just three methods, but one validates input, another sends emails, and the third writes to a log file. That's three unrelated concerns, so even with fewer methods, it violates SRP. The key is cohesion. All the methods in an SRP-compliant class should be working toward the same goal. One pitfall is thinking SRP means you need tiny classes with one method each. That would give you UserSaver, UserFinder, UserUpdater classes, which is absurdly granular and makes the codebase a nightmare to navigate. Focus on one responsibility, not one method. If every method in your class relates to the same concern, you're good, no matter how many there are.

speakable_v2.hook: SRP is about how many concerns a class has — not how many methods. Those are completely different things.

beats.text: SRP is about responsibility count, not method count. A class satisfies SRP as long as all its methods serve the same single concern — even if there are ten of them. The measure is cohesion of purpose, not lines of code.
The 'one method per class' misconception makes codebases absurdly fragmented. The real goal is that a class changes for one reason — and a class can have many methods all tied to that one reason.

items: UserRepository — has save(), findById(), update(), delete(). Four methods, one concern: data access for User entity.
Java String — has length(), substring(), toUpperCase(), contains(), and dozens more. One concern: string manipulation.
SRP violation — UserRepository also has sendWelcomeEmail(). Now it has two concerns: data access and notification.

beats.text: In a Spring Boot order module, OrderRepository might have findByStatus(), findByCustomerId(), save(), and deleteById() — all serve the same concern: persistence for Order. That's fine. The test is simple: do all these methods change together for the same reason? If yes, SRP holds. sharp edge: if two groups of methods in a class would change for different reasons — say, one group for DB schema changes and another for business rule changes — that's two responsibilities, regardless of how few methods there are.

items: Don't split every method into its own class — that creates fragmentation with no cohesion at all.
The question isn't 'how many methods?' but 'would all these methods change for the same reason?'
